claims.text: Increasing atomic size mismatch in refractory HEAs increases lattice distortion.
Targeted atomic-size mismatch produces lattice distortion through local chemical heterogeneity.
Enhanced lattice distortion creates internal strain fields that impede dislocation mobility.
Increased irradiation-induced lattice distortion associated with higher defect density limits plastic-zone expansion in TiZrHfNbMo0.1.
Creep deformation in the cited HfTaTiVZr and TaTiVWZr refractory HEAs is dislocation dominated over the tested 298–573 K range.
Increasing lattice distortion improves high-temperature creep resistance by reducing creep strain or creep rate.
Increasing lattice distortion raises high-temperature yield strength relative to a moderately distorted baseline alloy.
A single-phase BCC refractory HEA can retain high yield strength and resistance to softening at elevated temperatures.
Enhanced lattice distortion alters elastic moduli.
Increasing lattice distortion causes a distinct change in thermal expansion coefficients relative to the baseline.
Stress–strain curves and temperature-dependent expansion responses should shift systematically as lattice distortion increases if dislocation mobility governs deformation.
The proposed comparison uses incremental composition changes to vary atomic-size mismatch while holding other alloying and microstructural variables nearly constant.
The proposed tests cover steady-state creep and cyclic thermoelastic loading over approximately 300–800 °C.
Phase composition and grain size must be controlled to attribute response differences to lattice distortion.
The magnitude and threshold of the predicted mechanical and thermoelastic changes are not known.
Failure to observe statistically significant creep improvement or a distinct thermoelastic shift relative to the baseline would falsify the proposed governing role of lattice distortion.
